newsitem.title: USA: INSIGHT - U.S. retail stocks lag during holidays.
newsitem.headline: INSIGHT - U.S. retail stocks lag during holidays.

text.p: Retail stocks have lagged the market during the holiday season, despite prospects of improved fourth quarter profits, analysts said.

Retailers have kept inventories low and did not have to resort to the severe markdowns that characterized 1995's holiday season, analysts said. Jewelry and apparel sales were much improved from last year, analysts said.
"Retail stocks are doing worse than the rest of the market," said Dillon Read & Co Inc analyst Peter Schaeffer.
In recent weeks the Standard & Poor's Retail Index .RLX has lagged the Standard & Poor's 500 .SPC.

Prior to the start of Thanksgiving weekend, the Standard & Poors 500 index was 755.00 and the Standard & Poor's retailer index was 393.26 on November 27. Optimistic Thanksgiving sales reports pushed the retail index to 399.30 on December 3, but it has fallen to 365.02 on December 23.
In comparison, the Standard & Poor's 500 index has fallen less than five points to 750.66 at the end of December 23.
Both indices reflected market weakness starting December 11 and touched recent lows for the month on December 17, when the retail index fell to 365.02 and the Standard & Poor's 500 fell to 716.69.

TeleCheck Services reported earlier Tuesday that there was a 5.7 percent gain in same-store retail sales for the first 24 days of the Christmas shopping season. TeleCheck, a check acceptance company and unit of First Data Corp, based its figures on a year-over-year , same store comparison of the dollar volume of authorized checks.
Analysts have been expecting about a five percent increase in sales.
Schaeffer noted that the broader market rebounded while the retailers stayed lower. Both indices gained since early 1996 when retailer stocks were depressed.

Shares of major retailers such as Kmart Corp, Wal-Mart Stores Inc, Sears, Roebuck and Co, J.C. Penney Co Inc and Federated Department Stores Inc followed a pattern similar to the moves of the Standard & Poor's Retailing Index.
Saul Yaari, senior retailing analyst at Piper Jaffray Inc, said activity at department stores slowed after a strong start, while discount retailers have performed well this year.
Last year, retailers suffered weak fourth quarter profits from sharp markdowns after they aggressively built up inventory before the season, analysts said.
Apparel, shoes, jewelry and certain toys, such as Nintendo's new video game system and Tyco Toys Inc's Tickle Me Elmo, sold very well, Yaari said.
"Consumer electronics was a very poor category," Yaari said.
Those retailers were offering free computer accessories and generous financing terms to stir up sales, he said.

Maura Hunter Byrne, retailing analyst at J.P Morgan Securities who covers nine specialty apparel stocks, said she expects same-store sales to increase four to five percent and improved fourth quarter profits.

Most specialty retailers will not report their holiday sales results until early January, unlike major department stores that give weekly updates, Byrne said. Byrne noticed that retailers have not resorted to steep discounts to lure shoppers, Byrne said.

Byrne said the stores that will see the biggest improvements are AnnTaylor Stores Corp and Charming Shoppes Inc, which reported losses in last year's fourth quarter. Both chains have controlled their inventories and improved the selection of merchandise, Byrne said.
Also, the apparel retailing environment has turned around in spring 1995 and the trend has continued through the holiday season, Byrne said.
High consumer debt loads are expected to hurt retailers early next year, since shoppers will be repaying credit card bills, analysts said.

Regarding the outlook for retail stocks, Schaeffer said, "In 1997, there's no real reason for retailing to be strong." He cited the high levels of consumer debt and too many stores among the reasons why retailing as a sector will not be a compelling investment next year.
"It's just like it's been for the past couple of years," Schaeffer said. "Some stores will outperform others."
